sections.content: 21 (2008) reinvigorated the casino heist genre by grounding it in the true story of MIT students who used card counting to beat Vegas blackjack tables. Director Robert Luketic builds tension through mathematical precision rather than guns or violence, while Jim Sturgess leads a stellar young cast including Kate Bosworth and Aaron Yau. The film follows similar DNA to Ocean's Eleven (2001) and Casino (1995) but trades elaborate schemes for intellectual strategy. Kevin Spacey delivers a compelling performance as the manipulative professor Micky Rosa, showing how easily academic brilliance can be corrupted by greed.

sections.content: The success of 21 sparked renewed interest in gambling-focused dramas that explore the psychology of risk and addiction. Molly's Game (2017) delivered Aaron Sorkin's rapid-fire dialogue to the world of underground poker, while Mississippi Grind (2015) took a grittier look at compulsive gambling through stellar performances from Ryan Reynolds and Ben Mendelsohn. These films share DNA with classics like The Cincinnati Kid (1965), examining how the allure of easy money corrupts even the most disciplined minds.

Beyond pure gambling films, 21 connects to a broader category of academic-prodigies-turned-criminal stories. The Social Network (2010) similarly charts brilliant Harvard students corrupted by success, while War Dogs (2016) shows young entrepreneurs gaming the military industrial complex. These films tap into audiences' fascination with seeing exceptional minds use their talents for morally questionable ends. SUBHEAD: Math Genius Crime Stories

sections.content: The "brilliant minds turn to crime" subgenre gained momentum after 21, with films like The Imitation Game (2014) and A Beautiful Mind (2001) showing mathematical geniuses wrestling with moral choices. Searching for Bobby Fischer (1993) explores similar themes of prodigy and pressure in the chess world, while Good Will Hunting (1997) examines a mathematical genius who initially refuses to use his gifts constructively. These films share 21's fascination with exceptional intelligence as both blessing and curse.
